problem: Prior ObjectNav methods, both end-to-end RL (e.g., Zhu et al., Habitat-Web) and modular map-based ones (SemExp, PONI), have to learn semantic scene priors from scene datasets. That needs costly training (RL or interaction-free supervised) and the learned priors may not generalize well. No prior ObjectNav work used natural-language models as the source of the prior for choosing where to explore.
motivation: Humans find objects efficiently because they have common-sense knowledge of household layouts (e.g., a toilet is near a sink and bathtub). Pre-trained language models already encode this co-occurrence knowledge, so they can replace learned priors when choosing which frontier of a semantic map to explore next. This cuts training cost and aids generalization, including sim-to-real, since the modular map abstracts away raw-image noise.
key_idea: Describe the objects detected around each frontier of a semantic map as a sentence, then use a masked language model (RoBERTa-large) to score how relevant that frontier is to the target. Scoring is either zero-shot (sentence pseudo-likelihood) or feed-forward (a trained classifier head on sentence embeddings). The frontier chosen by this score, fused with a classic cost-utility frontier score, becomes the long-term goal for an FMM planner.
insight: The HM3D ablation (Table II) shows frontier-exploration design matters as much as the language prior. Cost-utility exploration alone, without the LM, already reaches SR 0.518, which beats the zero-shot LM variant (0.504). Adding the feed-forward LM head gives only +2.4 SR (0.542), and swapping cost-utility for nearest-frontier drops SR to 0.490. The biggest lever is perception: ground-truth semantic segmentation raises SR from 0.542 to 0.664 and SPL from 0.255 to 0.364, and the authors name segmentation errors as the main failure cause. The trained head beats zero-shot MLM scoring on both datasets, and it transfers from HM3D training data to Gibson.
method: Semantic map (SemExp-style): RGB-D plus pose are projected into a K×M×M top-down map (obstacle, explored and C_n semantic channels). Semantics come from a fine-tuned RedNet segmenter.

Frontier map (PONI-style): explored-area edge contours minus the dilated obstacle map, clustered into connected chains. Small clusters are removed, cluster centers become candidate frontiers, and each is scored with cost-utility S^CU = U(a) − λ·C(a) (Juliá et al.).

Frontier description with an entropy filter: objects inside a search window around each frontier are listed. Only the 15 lowest-entropy (most target-informative) object categories are kept; entropy comes from p(target|object) co-occurrence statistics computed on HM3D GT annotations.

Zero-shot scoring: for each target t_j, build the query "A frontier area containing o1,…,ok, t_j." and score it with frozen RoBERTa-large as an MLM. The frontier score is log p(W) for the actual target.

Feed-forward scoring: embed "This frontier contains o1,…,and ok." with RoBERTa-large and feed it to a 3-layer head that outputs |L_T| logits. The head is trained on HM3D room-level object lists (the target object in a room is the label, other objects are the input). The frontier score is the logit of the target.

Score fusion (Eq. 7): with bound B=[0.15,0.3] and S^CU normalized, use the LM score if max S^LLM > 0.3, the max of LM/CU scores if it falls within B, and the CU score alone if below 0.15. The selected frontier becomes the long-term goal.
Local policy: Fast Marching Method plans to the long-term goal and picks a nearby local goal, emitting discrete actions. No RL policy is learned.

setting.backbone: RoBERTa-large (frozen MLM for the zero-shot variant; RoBERTa-large sentence embeddings + trained 3-layer head for the feed-forward variant) + fine-tuned RedNet semantic segmentation; FMM planner
setting.training_data: No navigation-policy training. Feed-forward head is trained on object lists extracted from HM3D rooms (target object = label, other room objects = input). The informative-object list uses GT object co-occurrence statistics from HM3D annotations. RedNet segmentation is fine-tuned, following Ye et al. 2021. The zero-shot variant does no LM training.
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D (480×640) + base odometry/pose + goal category ID
setting.action_space: low-level discrete: MOVE_FORWARD 0.25 m, TURN_LEFT/RIGHT 30°, LOOK_UP/DOWN 30°, STOP (via frontier long-term goal + FMM local planner)
setting.privileged: none in the main results (simulator-provided odometry pose). One ablation row uses GT semantic segmentation.

numbers_note: The paper has only Table I (main results, Gibson + HM3D val) and Table II (HM3D ablation), and does not state episode counts. Metrics are printed as fractions (e.g., 0.542) and converted to percentages here; DTG is in meters. Omitted ablation rows: Exp only (no LLM) 0.518/0.244/4.084; Near + LLM 0.490/0.231/4.335. PONI has no HM3D result. The real-robot experiment (Jackal) is qualitative only.
results: L3MVN (Feed-forward) reaches SR 54.2 / SPL 25.5 on HM3D val, versus SemExp's 37.9 / 18.8, and SR 76.9 on Gibson val, versus PONI's 73.6 and SemExp's 65.2. The zero-shot variant reaches 50.4 on HM3D and 76.1 on Gibson. Despite the claim of beating all baselines, PONI's Gibson SPL (41.0) exceeds L3MVN's (38.8), and SemExp's HM3D DTG (2.943) is better than L3MVN's (3.934).
limitations: Perception is the main bottleneck: GT segmentation raises HM3D SR from 54.2 to 66.4, and segmentation errors are cited as the main failure cause.

The language gain is modest and the zero-shot variant is weak. Cost-utility exploration without any LM (SR 51.8) beats the zero-shot LM variant (50.4), and the 'LLM' is a 355M masked LM scoring only object-co-occurrence sentences.

Efficiency is not uniformly better (Gibson SPL below PONI; HM3D DTG worse than SemExp). The real-world evaluation is qualitative, and the zero-shot variant still relies on HM3D co-occurrence statistics and in-domain fine-tuned segmentation.
